entries.text: A master in from the Canche says the prefect there pays for true word of any sail seen off the river mouths, and remembers who brought it.
The sealed ship

An English ship lies roped to a post on the bank with the toll's seal on her hatch, by the king's order against English merchants. Her wool is spoiling under the hatch and her master counts the days aloud.
Forty-one days. I landed on the wrong day, they roped her to that post, and the wool has sweated under the hatch ever since. Count with me, Frisian. It passes the time.
Still here. So is the seal. So is the smell. Sit down, I have a new number for you.
You turned my wool when my own king's friends would not look at it. I have told three crews. One of them believed me.
The man who bought my wool at a rotting price. Fair enough. It was rotting. Sit down anyway.
He is my mother's sister's son and he eats like two of them. The abbot has not said no. In this town that is nearly yes.
Lend him your crew for a day to turn and air the wool
With the clerk's leave and his boy counting, your men haul the sacks up through the hatch and spread them on the grass. Half is past saving. Half is not, and Leofstan knows who made the difference.
Buy six sacks at a rotting price

Three pennies a sack for wool worth eight when sound. The clerk lets it pass: an Englishman may not sell here, but nothing says a Frisian may not buy. Leofstan counts the coins twice and thanks you once.
Hear him out and tell him what wool fetches at Dorestad
He listens to the price as a hungry man listens to a list of dishes. It costs you an hour, and he has a new number to be angry about.

A roped English ship on a mud bank at low water, her hatch sealed with wax and cord; sacks of wool spread to air on the grass, a big fair skipper counting on his fingers at a Frisian, a clerk's boy with a tally stick; grey morning.
Two to swear with him

At the toll house a Frisian shipmaster is charged with declaring thirty bolts of cloth and landing forty. He may clear himself by oath if two men of his own trade swear that his oath is good, and he has found one.
You know me from the Rhine, or near enough. Thirty bolts I said and thirty there were. Stand beside me and say I am a man whose oath is good. That is all the law asks.
The law asks that he swear, and that two swear he is no perjurer. It does not ask whether they counted his bolts. I counted them. I only mention it.
You stood beside a short tally once. I have it on wax.
The man who asks for a count before an oath. Come in. There are few of you.
Swear with him

The three of you swear on the relics from Saint Peter's, and the clerk writes 'cleared', slowly. Outside, the Frisian presses twenty pennies on you, which is more than an honest man would have needed to.
On the way to the relics the clerk has the bolts counted again, aloud, on the bank. Forty. The Frisian pays his fine, and you pay yours for the oath you were about to swear.
Ask the clerk to count the bolts again before anyone swears
Hildric counts with pleasure. There are forty. Nobody swears anything, the Frisian pays, and the clerk remarks that a man who asks for a count is rarer than a man who offers an oath.
Say you do not know him well enough
He finds his second man by evening, a wine seller who owes him. You hear later that it went through. You also hear what the wine seller was paid.

Inside a timber toll house: a thin tonsured clerk with wax tablets behind a table, a sweating Frisian shipmaster with his hand out towards a small reliquary, a second merchant hanging back by the door; bolts of cloth stacked outside in the light.
The moneyer's pot
Only the king's new heavy penny passes now. The moneyer takes old and foreign silver into his pot and gives back new pennies, less his cut, and he cuts less for silver that comes to him sorted.
Put it on the bench. All of it. English, old Frankish, cut pieces, that thing with the hole. I weigh, I say a loss, and then you may be sad.
The Frisian who sorts. Sit. Your silver comes to me like a decent family: I know who everyone is.
You tried me with a light one. I have not forgotten. I have not minded either. Do it to the man at Dorestad.
My sister's son sends word by you? The reverse die is cracking, and he has a coin he cannot read. The first I knew. The second he would do well to keep quiet about.
The moneyer at Dorestad says my pennies run light. I keep one of his in this pouch. Weigh it yourself. Go on.
Spend the evening sorting it first: good from doubtful, English from old

You sort by lamplight until your eyes water. In the morning he weighs each pile once and takes two pennies in forty where he would have taken four. He says nothing kind. He pours you ale, which from him is the same.
Tip the purse out as it is
He weighs, files one piece, sniffs another, and names his loss: four in forty. The new pennies are broad and bright and all alike, which is the point of them.
Slip one light penny in, to see whether he is as good as he says
He picks it out of forty by the ring it makes on the bench, without looking, and sets it down in front of you. Then he takes his four pennies as usual. Now you know who is weighing your silver.
Keep your silver and ask what the king has ordered about the coin

The new penny is to be taken in every place, town and market, he says, and a free man who refuses it pays fifteen shillings. The old ones are silver and nothing more. He says it like a man reading out his own good fortune.
A low smoky mint: a thick-armed moneyer in a scorched leather apron at a bench with a small hand balance, piles of mixed silver sorted by lamplight, a crucible glowing behind him; evening.
Sails off the bar
On the long street a wine seller is telling everyone that heathen ships lie off the river mouth. The pilots have stopped taking boats over the bar, and three masters have decided to wait.
Six of them, long and low, with the masts down. A shepherd saw them from the dunes at first light. Nobody sails today who loves his children.
It is the same ones that fell on the holy island in the north. Depend on it.
I have not seen them. I have not seen the shepherd either. But I am not paid to be the first to find out.
Sail on the ebb anyway

Off the river mouth there are six boats, long and low, with the masts down: herring men from Boulogne lying to their nets. Yours is the only wine keel to cross this week, and the Kentish side will pay for it.

No pilot will come, and you touch on the bar going out: a wet hour with poles and bad words. From the last of the sand you can see the six terrible ships. They are herring boats from Boulogne, lying to their nets.
Find out who saw them

The shepherd has no name and no flock. The wine seller has a rival whose casks were to cross on this tide and reach the Kentish buyers first. By evening the whole street knows it, and the pilots are working again.
Wait three days with the rest

Three days of ale and counting. On the fourth a herring boat from Boulogne comes in and her master asks what everyone is afraid of. Six boats, long and low, with the masts down: his, and his cousins'.

A long muddy street of plank houses and stalls: a red-faced wine seller on a cask with both arms spread, a knot of shipmasters listening, a pilot leaning on his pole and looking at the sky; bright windy morning.
Once I was water
Saint-Germain's monk on the abbeys' row sells wine by the cask and riddles by the leaf. One leaf is Bishop Aldhelm's, in Latin, and he says it is the first of four.
Wine is fifty the cask and I will not move. A riddle is twelve pennies and I will not move on that either. But the riddle keeps longer.
You have had my leaf a while. Once I was water, full of scaly fish. Well? What am I now?
Salt! Of course salt. Then the next leaf is where salt is made. I sent it to the brother who rakes the pans on the island south of the Loire.
You paid me in a riddle last time and I have not slept well since.
Four years on this mud bank. I sell wine like a Frisian and the cellarer sends me more wine and no leave to come home. A man needs something to think about.
Buy the leaf
A strip of parchment in a round hand: once water teeming with fish, tormented by fire, now most like snow. It is Latin. He reads it to you twice and will not read it a third time without wine.
Give him the answer

He gives you half your pennies back, which he says is the custom of the school, and the name of the next keeper: Natalis, who rakes salt on Saint Philibert's island and cannot hand over a sack without a question.
Set him a riddle of your own
You set him one from the north. He walks up and down the row with it for an hour, comes back without the answer, and sells nothing all day out of pure distraction. He counts it a fair trade.
Not today
He shrugs and tucks the leaf back into his sleeve. 'It will keep,' he says. 'That is its nature.'

A round-faced monk in a wine-stained travelling cowl on the step of a storehouse, holding up a strip of parchment between two fingers; casks behind him, the abbey's sealed letter in a tube on his chest; noon.
Salt for the abbey's fish
Saint-Germain's man needs bay salt for the abbey's fish before the autumn, and his usual carrier has not come back from the south.
Ten sacks of grey salt from the bay, before Michaelmas. The island sells it for nothing and the sea charges the rest. I pay half as much again as the street.
Ask for Brother Natalis on the pans, or old Vitalis in the store. Say Meginbert sent you. Say it before they ask you a riddle, or you will be there till dark.
You took my order for salt. I have counted the days since. So has the fish.
Take the order: ten sacks before Michaelmas

He cuts a tally stick, splits it and gives you half. Ten sacks, half as much again as the street pays. He adds that the abbey's letter passes its own goods without the tenth, and looks at the toll house as he says it.
Take it, and ask for a cask of the abbey's wine on account
He gives you the cask and takes it out of the premium, to the penny. A monk who has sold wine for four years on a mud bank is not out-bargained before noon.
Tell him what salt fetched at Dorestad, and leave it
He writes the Dorestad price on his tablet, says it is robbery, and asks whether you know anyone else going south.
A storehouse door on a row of abbey houses: a monk splitting a tally stick with a small knife, an empty fish barrel upended beside him, a Frisian holding out his hand for his half; afternoon sun.
A fast day at the cell
It is a fast day. The cell of Saint Josse feeds whoever is waiting on the wind, on fish, pulses and bread, and the guest hall is full.
Thanks be to God. Come in, there is room on the bench if you breathe in. No meat, no cheese, and before you ask, the eels count as fish.
Half of these are not waiting for a ship. They are waiting for a harvest. I feed them the same. The Rule does not ask where a guest is going.
Your herring fed forty. I told them it came from a Frisian. They prayed for you anyway.
While we wait: a daughter of a fair forest, crowded with companions, running on many roads and leaving no track. I shall be in England before you have it.
Give a barrel of herring to the kitchen

Osmund has the barrel opened before it is off your shoulder. Forty people eat herring who expected beans. He writes nothing down: he says the cell's book is for the dead and the kitchen is for the living.
Leave six pennies for pulses
He counts them into the alms dish in front of the hall, so that the giving is seen and the amount is not. Beans tomorrow, he says, and the day after.
Sit down to the fast with them and take the cleric's riddle

Bean pottage, a heel of bread, and a reading from a book Osmund has read aloud nine times. The cleric scratches his three lines on your tablet. Your crew fast with the rest and are surprisingly quiet about it.

A crowded timber guest hall on a grey Lenten day: long benches, wooden bowls of pottage, a broad stooped monk with a ladle at the door, a young cleric scratching on a wax tablet; rain beyond the open door and a wet river bank.
The bag and the answer

At the cell a tall English monk has been turning ships down for a month. He carries a letter from Alcuin for the bishop of the holy island and a small bag of alms to buy back the boys the heathen carried off. He needs a ship going north, and he is afraid of ships.
Forgive me. You are bound for the Rhine mouth? In a boat of that size? Forgive me again. How many days, and does she roll?
The letter is for Bishop Higbald. The bag is for the boys who were taken from Saint Cuthbert's. My master will speak to the king for them. I am to carry the answer, and I am a month late already.
He has refused four ships. One was too small, one too large, one had a master who whistled. Take him, of your charity, before he refuses the weather.
You asked to hear my master's letter. Most men ask what is in the bag.
Take him to Dorestad, where the Frisian ships go north

He pays eighteen pennies of passage from his own purse, not the bag, and comes aboard holding the letter case over his head like a man fording a river. On the way he tells you the boys' names, and what the bishop will give for each.
Ask to hear what his master wrote about the raid

He reads you a copy of Alcuin's letter to the king of the Northumbrians and puts it into plain speech as he goes: that no such dread was ever seen in Britain before, and that nobody thought such a voyage could be made. He lets you keep the leaf. He has it by heart.
Tell him which Frisian masters go north, and when
You give him three names and the month each sails. He writes them on his tablet, thanks you, apologises for thanking you at such length, and goes back to watching the river with dislike.

A tall stooping English monk in a patched black cowl on a river bank, a leather letter case clutched under one arm and a small sealed bag in his fist, looking with open distrust at a very small boat; a broad older monk behind him with his hands spread; flat morning light.
The old deacon

An old English priest who says Mass at the cell some Sundays was at York twenty years ago, when a Frisian merchant killed a nobleman's son and every Frisian in the city took ship for home. He was on that ship.
I was a deacon then. My master sent me down the river with the Frisians, to see young Liudger safe home with his books. Nobody on that ship spoke until we were over the bar.
It was a brawl, not a murder. A boy of good kin, a Frisian with a knife, and too much ale between them. But the dead boy's kin did not ask which it was.
No blood-price was ever paid that I heard of. A thing like that does not grow smaller in a chest.
Ask who struck the blow, and whose son he killed

He gives you the dead boy's father's name, and the name of the kinsman who still asks after Frisians at York: Ecgwulf. The merchant's name he gives last and lowest. You have seen it before, at Dorestad, cut over a storehouse door.
Ask after Liudger and his books

Liudger is a priest among the East Frisians now, he says, and the books got home dry, because Putul sat on the chest the whole way. He tells it as the chief deed of his life, and perhaps it was. The rest of the story comes out with it.
Leave the old man to his office
He nods and turns back to the altar. He has kept it twenty years. He can keep it until you next ask.

A small bare chapel beside a guest hall: a very old priest with a white tonsure folding an altar cloth, one candle, a Frisian standing with his cap in his hand; through the door, a river and masts; Sunday morning.
Six to carry

An English pilgrim bound for Rome has died in the ale-house, waiting for his party. He is to be buried at Saint Peter's this evening, and there are not enough men in the street who knew him to carry the bier.
He was three nights under my roof, so by my own people's law I answer for him. I did not think it would mean this. He has a wife at Dofras and a bundle I have not opened.
Six to carry, a penny for the wax, and a name to say. I have the name. I am short of the six.
Carry him with your crew
Your four and two English hands carry him up the street behind the cross. The priest says the name three times. Afterwards the house feeds all six and notches nothing on the tally.
Pay for the wax and a Mass
Two candles instead of one, and a Mass on the seventh day. The priest writes the name in the church's book with yours beside it as the giver, spelled as a Frank spells Frisian names.
Offer to see his bundle and the news across to his wife at Dofras
She ties the bundle with her own cord and tells you the wife's name and her brother's boat on the strand at Dofras. It is a small weight in the hold and you are aware of it the whole way.

Dusk on a street of plank houses: six men carrying a plain bier on poles behind a wooden cross, a tall woman in a linen head-cloth walking after with a tied bundle, a small timber church ahead with its door open and one candle inside.
Wulfgifu's fire

Wulfgifu keeps the house where the men from over the sea lodge, and answers to the toll for every guest. By her fire sits a Kentish hand who was put ashore here and wants a berth on anything that sails.
From Dorestad, by the cut of the boat. Four of you, and not all of one people. Sit by the fire. I answer to the toll for my guests, so I like to look at them.
Your bench is kept. I told a Frank it was broken.
The lad you took: does he still eat like that? His mother asks, by every boat.
No English keels again this moon but my cousin's, and his is growing roots.
I can row, reef and cook, and I know the Wantsum and the Thames mouth. I am tired of this bank. Say a wage.
Take the hand on

He has his bundle on his shoulder before you have finished the sentence. Wulfgifu tells him to mind the master, and tells you his mother's name and village, so that you know there is someone to answer to.
Stand the bench a round and listen

By the second cup you know who crossed this week and what was said. Wine is short on the Kentish side, and the first cask over will be paid for like the last one at a wedding. Three men say it, separately.
Sit by the fire and say little
She asks where you have come from and already knows. You answer anyway. It is warm, nobody wants anything from you for an hour, and that is worth something on this coast.

A low smoky ale-house with a central hearth: a tall woman in a blue gown with one small round brooch at the throat and a ladle, benches of English and Frisian shipmen, a young sailor with a bundle between his feet looking up hopefully; night, firelight.
The schoolmaster's books
Osmund has two of Saint-Wandrille's books on his shelf, lent by the schoolmaster there and long overdue. The schoolmaster has asked for them by your boat.
Harduin sent you. I knew he would send somebody in the end. I had hoped for a slower boat.
One you may have now. The other I am reading aloud in the guest hall, and we have reached the part with the whale. Would you take a man's whale from him?
Take the one and leave him his whale

He wraps the book in a sealskin, then in sacking, then tells you three times to stow it above the bilge. The other, he says, will follow when the whale has been dealt with, by Michaelmas or the one after.
Take both: a loan is a loan
He hands over the second book with a finger still in his place. The guest hall will never know what became of the whale. He blesses your boat all the same, a little shortly.
Give him until you next call
He promises to read faster. You both know he will not.
A monk's cell with a shelf of five books: a broad stooped monk clutching one book to his chest and holding out another, wrapped in sealskin, at arm's length; a Frisian waiting with both hands open.
Corbie's man
Corbie's man on the abbeys' row takes the exile's letter without surprise. In eight days he is back from the Somme with a book the length of a hand, sewn in oiled linen.
From the island. Do not say from whom: I can see the knot. Come back in eight days, and until then you sold me wax.

This is the old abbot's own writing on how a house should be ordered: who keeps the mill, how many loaves, where the bees stand. He wants it by him to finish. Keep it above the bilge and below notice.
Take the book south
He gives you twelve pennies for the carrying and a cake of wax to show at the toll, since you sold him wax. The book goes into your sea chest, inside a shoe.
Take it, and let the toll clerk look at it first

Hildric unpicks the stitching, reads forty leaves about bees, granaries and the porter's duties, and sews it up again nearly as it was. He pays thirty pennies for the count at Nantes, who pays him. Nobody is any wiser, and one more man knows your boat.
Tell him the letter was all you agreed to
He nods and puts the book back into his sleeve. Another boat will be found by summer. He buys nothing from you, and says the wax was very good.

A shut storehouse room lit by one high window: a tall grave monk holding out a small book sewn in oiled linen, a cake of wax on the table between him and a Frisian; outside the door, the shadow of someone passing.
The prefect's question
Grippo, the king's prefect of the port, asks every master the same thing: whether there is a blade, a mail coat or a horse aboard that might find its way to a Northman.
I was in a storm off this coast once, near dawn, and vowed to the saints of the Seine if I lived. I lived. I paid on Christmas Eve. So you see I keep accounts. What is under the hides?
By the king's edict, the man who sells a Northman mail, arms or a horse dies for it. I did not write it. I read it out.
You sit low for a wool boat.
You opened your hold to me unasked last time. I remember a thing like that for about ten years.
Open the hold and let his men look
His men lift two hides, knock on a cask and climb out again. Grippo says a word to the toll table as he goes. The tenth is lighter on you for a season, and nobody says why.
Tell him what sails you have seen, and where

He hears you out without a word, asks the day twice, and has a clerk write it. Then he pays you eight pennies, as a man pays a debt, and asks whether the house was here before the fire. He is looking for the ones that were.
Swear there is nothing, and keep the hatch shut
He looks at you for the length of a Pater Noster and then at your waterline. Then he lets you go. He does not believe you. He has six other boats to disbelieve before dark.
He has the hatch off before the oath is out of your mouth. What is found is carried up the bank under guard, and your name goes on a tablet that will be read at the next king's court.

A grey weathered officer with a long moustache and a red cloak standing at the edge of a river bank, one boot on a small boat's gunwale, looking down into her hold; two armed men behind him, burnt house plots between standing houses beyond; cold clear light.
The man who asks for the Weser

At dusk a man comes down to the strand from the row of huts on the abbey's land. He is one of the king's Saxons, moved here with his people and a priest set over them. He asks whether any ship goes to the Weser.
Weser. You know it? There are four of us. I have no silver. I can row, I can mend, I can carry. I can be quiet.
They gave us a priest and a field. The field is good. It is not ours.
I need hands at the east stream and I do not ask where hands were born. But I will not hide a man from the count. Say he is mine openly, or not at all.
Take the four aboard at night, for the IJssel and the road east

They come down in the dark with one bundle between them and lie under the sailcloth until the cliffs are astern. It is against the king's order, and everyone aboard knows it. Brunger, if he sails with you, rows like two men and says nothing at all.
Speak for him at the slip, where the wright needs hands

The wright takes him on before the priest, in daylight, with words said. He stays, as the king ordered, and his children will grow up speaking Romance. Ever after, the wright at the east stream mends your boat before the others.
Tell him truly that no ship here goes so far
He nods as if he had known. He asks which way the river runs to the sea, looks at it a while, and goes back up to the huts before the priest counts heads.

Dusk under a Roman city wall of robbed stone: a gaunt man in undyed wool standing at the water's edge with his hands open, three figures waiting far back by a row of identical huts, a small boat on the strand with her crew looking at their master.
Angilwin's chalk
The toll man at the river gate chalks every cask himself and cannot be hurried. Three boats are waiting on him, and the flood is making.
Four boats, one tollman, and the tide will bring a fifth whether I hurry or not. So I do not hurry. Yours is the small one. I have you.
Fewer casks every autumn the quarrel lasts. Why are the ports shut? The lord abbot keeps King Offa's letters in a chest downriver and calls him his dearest friend. That is all a tollman is told.
Last time you said what you had before I asked. I chalk such boats first. Do not tell the others why.
The boat with the interesting ballast. I shall chalk slowly today. Sit.
The priest set over the Saxons was here, asking which boats left on which tide. I told him the tide. It is true of every boat.
Wait your turn
He chalks the three boats ahead of you, each cask, each top, and then yours in a quarter of the time, because there is less of it. The flood has an hour left in it. He knew that.
Ask him why the ports are shut to the English

The king has shut his shores to English merchants, and theirs are shut to his. No Frank is to buy of them and none of them is to land. A Frisian, he says, chalking, is a thing the order forgot to mention.
Hold his tally sticks and call the casks for him

A master calling casks like a toll boy is a thing the other masters enjoy a good deal. Angilwin enjoys it too, without showing it, and chalks your own casks with a lighter hand than the law quite intends.

A river gate in an old stone wall, the tide brimming at its foot: a long thin toll man with a drooping moustache chalking a cask top, tally sticks under his arm, four boats waiting nose to tail and their masters watching the water rise.
The cooper's mallet
The cooper in the market place knocks on a cask without being asked, listens, and tells the owner what is wrong with it. He is owed money upriver and has a cask to sell.
Hear that? Dull. That one is drinking its own wine through the staves. Full to the bung and tight in the hoop, or you carry vinegar to the English.
They are going up for the fair by the dozen and every hoop on the river is slack. I have not sat down since Saint Ouen's.
The cellarer of Saint Denis owes me for last autumn's hooping. He pays at the fair, he says. He says it every fair. If you go up, say Ursio asked. Say it where the abbot can hear.
He paid! In front of the abbot, they tell me, and went the colour of his own wine. I have a cask here that was going to be yours anyway.
Buy the sound cask a buyer left with him

Last year's wine from a left-bank grower, in a cask he hooped himself and will answer for. Thirty-eight pennies, because the man who ordered it went home without it. He knocks on it once more to let you hear.
Promise to say his name to the cellarer at the fair
He tells you the sum, the number of casks, and the exact words the cellarer used last October. You are to repeat them. He makes you say them back.
Take the cask he kept for you
He rolls it down to the strand himself and stows it bung up. It is his wife's sister's best ale-house wine, he says, and she does not know it is gone.
Ask which cellar's wine is sound this year

He knows each cellar by its hoops. The abbey's new wine is thin this year and there is a great deal of it: it will go cheap at the fair to whoever asks second. The old wine is another matter, and he says whose.

A market place inside a city wall: a short thick-armed cooper with dark curling hair bent to a cask with his ear against it and a mallet raised, willow hoops stacked beside him, a Frisian with his arms folded; morning.
Good day, in a riddle
A canon of the cathedral, its chief singer, greets strangers with a riddle in place of good day. He writes it on a wax tablet for anyone who cannot answer, and for anyone who can.
Bound together with iron I am bound, and bound I bind in turn. Good day. Well?
You still have my tablet. Wax is not free. Neither is the answer.
A chain. Yes. You may now say good day like other people, though I shall think less of you for it.
The abbot's new school downriver wants calfskin, and Saint-Denis buys it by the bundle at the October fair. The abbot sings better than any man on the river and counts better than he sings.
Take the tablet
Three lines of Latin pressed into green wax in a hand as neat as his singing. He hums while he writes. He says it is an easy one, for a man who has ever moored a boat.
Answer him
He is so pleased that he takes you into the choir and reads you a leaf of the antiphoner, pointing at each word as he says it. The boys stop fighting over the book long enough to stare.
Ask him what a book is worth

The skins of a herd, he says, and a year of a man's eyes: three fingers hold the pen and the whole body aches. Then to whom: a church that lacks it will pay what a church that has two would laugh at. He names four churches, and what each lacks.

The porch of a cathedral made of two churches joined by a gallery: a small round-shouldered canon with a grey tonsure and a bone stylus behind his ear, holding out a wax tablet; two choir boys peering round a pillar.
Nine years of psalms
The abbot of Saint-Denis has asked, by your boat as by every boat, for the psalter the cathedral's chief singer borrowed nine years ago.
Nine years? It cannot be nine. It is nine. I know exactly where it is. That has never been the difficulty.
The boys learn their psalms from it. If it goes, they fight over one book again. Tell the abbot it is being used, which is more than he did with it.
Ask for it plainly, in the abbot's name
He wraps it in a sealskin himself. The choir boys line the porch to watch it go down to the strand, as for a burial. He does not say goodbye to you. He says it to the book.
Pay for skins, so the boys can copy what they need first

Half a bundle of calfskin from the schoolmaster downriver, and a fortnight of boys with ink to the elbows. Then the old book goes into your boat with Hildhard's own blessing on it, and the cathedral has a psalter that is nobody's but its own.
Leave it with him and tell the abbot it is in use
He promises to write to the abbot himself, a long letter, in his best hand. It will go by another boat. You have the feeling it will arrive in about nine years.
A choir with one great book on a stand and three boys leaning over it: a small canon with his hand flat on the open page, looking at a Frisian as at a bailiff; coloured light from a high window.
The table at the gate
It is a hungry year. Outside the wall the brothers of Saint Peter's ladle pottage at a table by their gate, and the row before it reaches the old graves.
Rye, barley, beans, anything that swells in water. I pay what the abbey allows when I have it, and God's price when I have not. What is in the boat?
It stood in the field like other corn, ears and all. You put your hand to it and it was dust. I saw it. Ask anyone from our vill.
The law now says no food leaves the realm. It does not say how it is to get from the boat to the pot. That part is left to us.
The Frisian who gave rye. We said your name at the table. They did not know what a Frisian was, so I said: a man with a boat.
Give two sacks of rye to the table
Two sacks is pottage for the whole row for three days, thick enough to stand a spoon in. The brother asks your name and your saint, and you have to think about the second.
Sell him two sacks at the monk's price
Six pennies for what the market inside the wall would give twenty for. He counts them out one at a time, in case you change your mind between pennies. You do not.
Leave five pennies for the pot
He thanks you and says that silver cannot be eaten, but that it can be shown to the archbishop's steward, who has a full barn and likes to be shown silver.
Stand by the row a while and listen

They talk of the corn that was dust, and of a harvest that must come because it has always come. Nobody asks you for anything. That is the worst of it, and your crew are quiet all the way back to the boat.

A monastery gate outside a city wall, stone coffins on the slope behind: a brother ladling pottage at a trestle table, a long silent row of thin people with bowls, a Frisian crew standing awkwardly to one side; cold early light.
A stick on Adalsind's wall
Adalsind keeps the ale-house inside the river gate and a notched stick for every shipman who ever drank there. She knows who is in harbour and what wine fetched at the fair before the toll man does.
New boat, old trade. Sit. I cut a stick for every master: one notch a cup. You may pay now or when you sail. Nobody has yet paid never.
Your stick is clean. I keep it by the door to shame the others.
Six notches. I counted them out to the toll man last night, for something to do.
The boats are down from the fair full to the thwarts. Wine is dear over the sea until Christmas: every Englishman who lodges here says so, and they do not agree about much.

My Englishman is back with wool cloth to sell: Leofstan of Hamwic, not the loud one on the Canche. The cloaks, he says, are to be made long again. The king complained he could not cover himself in bed with one.
Pay what is notched
She takes the three pennies, bites one from habit, and shaves your notches off with her knife so the stick is white again. A clean stick, she says, is the best lodging letter on this river.
Ask what wine is fetching over the sea

She gives you three skippers' words, the day each said it and how drunk he was. They agree: the West Saxon shore is short of wine and will stay so until the last fair boats have crossed. It is true, and it will not be true for long.
Drink on the stick and settle next time
She cuts the notches a little deeper than she needs to and hangs your stick where the door lets the light fall on it.

A timber ale-house built against the inside of a Roman wall: a broad red-armed woman with a ladle and a notching knife on a cord, a wall hung with tally sticks, a toll man asleep by the fire; evening.
The moneyer's tray
The young moneyer at Rotomagus keeps a private tray of every strange coin he was meant to melt. One of them is thin broad silver with writing like bird tracks and no king's face.
This came in a Dane's purse. Good silver: I nicked it. No cross, no king, no letters I know. I should have melted it. Do not tell my uncle on the Canche.
You have seen one before? Then say what it is, and I will say what I would give for another.
And tell my uncle his reverse die is cracking. I strike with what he sends. If the pennies come out ugly, it is the Canche's ugliness.
Tell him what it is

A coin of the Saracens' king, you tell him, come up the rivers of the east and paid for in furs and people; north of the Danes' wall they weigh them like any lump. He pays six pennies for the knowledge and puts the coin back on the tray, in the middle.
Hold it, and ask what the Dane said

It is lighter than it looks and rings true on the bench. The Dane said it came from the east, a year's journey, and that where he had it they were as common as fish scales. Gerold did not believe him. He is beginning to.
Promise to carry his word to the Canche
The reverse die is cracking, he repeats, from the cross outward. And nothing about the tray. He makes you say back the part that is to be left out.

A cramped mint: a wiry soot-armed young man holding a wooden tray of odd coins under a shuttered window, one broad thin coin held up to a crack of light between finger and thumb, a hammer and dies on the block behind him.
Skins for the school
A tide below the city, at Saint-Wandrille's landing, the master of the abbot's new school wants calfskin for his boys and his books, and has two books out on loan that have not come home.
Parchment. Clean, scraped both sides, no holes a boy can put his finger through. Saint-Denis takes the best at the fair. I will take the next best and thank you for it.
The English guest-master at Saint Josse has two of my books. He is a good man and a slow reader. If you call at the Canche, ask for them with your hand out.
Is that parchment under the sailcloth? Bring it into the light. No, do not unroll it with those hands.
Your leaves had no holes. I looked for them. The boys have since made some.
Take his order: four bundles from the fair
Four bundles of a hundred, before the spring. He writes the order on a scrap, reckons the price twice by two different roads, gets the same sum both times and is visibly content.
Sell him the parchment you carry

He counts the hundred leaves and holds each one to the light. It takes most of an hour. Then he pays seventy pennies without a word of bargaining, which the abbey's cellarer will hear about at chapter.
Promise to ask Osmund for the books
He tells you their names, their size, the colour of the boards and which has a wormhole through the first six leaves. He says to wrap them in sealskin, then sacking, and to stow them above the bilge.
Let him check your reckoning

He goes down your tally with a dry finger and finds that a wine seller at the fair gave you short change by three pennies. He is right. He writes the working out for you, so that you can show the man next October.

A lead-roofed abbey in a wooded valley by the river, a small jetty: an old thin monk with a white tonsure and a ruling board under his arm holding a leaf of parchment up against the sky, a Frisian boat tied below him.
Books come home
The schoolmaster of Saint-Wandrille has seen your boat from the jetty and is already walking down, with his hands washed.
From the Canche? Then you have my books, or a reason. I have heard a great many reasons.
Both? He gave up the one he was reading? What did you do, take it out of his hands?
Hand over a book

He smells the book before he opens it and says it has been in a dry boat. Twenty-four pennies for the carrying, and a place on the abbey's jetty whenever you want one. The other book, he says, he will believe in when he sees it.
Hand over both books

He counts the gatherings in each, finds the wormhole where he left it, and pays forty pennies. Then he sits down on the jetty and writes Osmund a letter of thanks so courteous that it will take the man a week to see what it means.
Tell him the books are gone
He hears you to the end. Then he asks which one had the wormhole, as if it mattered now, and walks back up to the school. No church on the river gives your boat a book again while he lives.

An abbey jetty at slack water: an old monk kneeling on the planks with a book open on his knees, his nose almost touching the page, a sealskin wrapper and a length of sacking beside him, a Frisian waiting with his cap off.
The clerk's list

A clerk of the cathedral keeps a list of everyone carried off from the city since the fire, and what was last heard of each. He asks one thing of every shipman who goes north: to carry a name and ask after it.
I write the name on a strip, with the trade the person had and what the church will pay. They change the names. Listen for the trade: a girl who can weave, a clerk who can write.
They came on a feast, up the tide, and nobody had shut a gate. If you go to the Loire, I have a letter for the bishop at Nantes that says only that.
There is a fleet on the island at Oissel, a short pull above us. I know who speaks for it. I could wish I did not need to.
You brought me a true word last time. A family can live on a true word. It cannot live on none.
Take a strip north
A strip of parchment the width of two fingers: a name, a trade, a sum. He does not thank you much. He shows you how long the list is, so that you understand it is not ingratitude.
Put twenty pennies in the ransom chest
He weighs them, writes the sum against no name in particular, and says it is half a weaver or a third of a deacon. He says it in the voice he uses for the price of wax, and dislikes himself for it.
Take his letter for the bishop at Nantes
One leaf, sealed with the cathedral's seal on a strip of the same burnt stuff as his sleeve. It says what he saw in May of 841, in order, without one adjective.
Tell him what fleets you have seen, and where

He writes it down exactly and gives you the same in return: which fleet lies where on the river this month, who speaks for it, and what it has lately been buying. It is the best word on the lower Seine, and it is free.

A fire-scarred cathedral patched with unburnt timber: a spare clerk going grey early, a burn scar up his left forearm, unrolling a long stitched roll of parchment strips across a table; a single lamp.
The market on the mud
A fleet's quartermaster is selling on the mud under the wall what was taken upriver: plate, cloth and people. He takes silver by weight and wine by the cask.
Silver on the scale. Wine also good. This cup, this cloth, this woman who weaves, that man who writes. All cheap. We go before the moon.
Your king says death for selling us horses and mail. Good. I am not buying horses. I am selling cups.
The man who writes is a deacon of this city. He is on my list. Forty pennies' weight, the Dane says, and it is fair as he sees it. I have twenty.
Make up the clerk's silver and buy the deacon back

The Dane weighs your pennies with the clerk's, nods, and cuts the rope with the same knife he eats with. The deacon walks up the strand without looking back. The clerk draws a line through a name and writes two words beside it.
Buy the cup with the cross hammered flat
Sixty pennies for a cup worth four times that to the church it came from. It cannot be sold in a Christian market without a story. The clerk watches you stow it and says nothing, exactly.
Sell him a cask for silver by weight
He pays in hacked silver, half as much again as the fair gives, and asks when you will be back. From the wall, people who have someone missing can see your boat among theirs.
Walk on along the wall
You keep your eyes on the stones of the wall, one of which is built in upside down. The weaver on the mud is still looking at you when you reach the gate.

Low tide under a Roman wall: long ships drawn up, a Dane with a folding scale squatting among cups, bolts of cloth and three roped people; a clerk with a small chest standing in the mud in his good shoes; overcast.
A cask from a guest's boat
In the night a cask was lifted out of your boat under the wall. This is Rollo's city now, with one lord and one law, and a theft from a guest can be laid before him in his hall.
The count hears thefts himself. He hangs the thief, and the man who knew of it and kept quiet. Be sure of what you say before you say it.
They say he hung gold rings on an oak in the forest for three years and nobody touched them. I have not seen the oak. I have seen the gallows.
A cask. From a guest's boat. In my river. Who else came up behind you? Say that first. Then the cask.
You told me true about the sails. Your casks are chalked light while I live.
Lay the theft before him

Your lookout names the boat he saw against the wall. By noon the cask is back, unbroached, and a man you never see again is led out through the east gate. Nobody in the market steals so much as an apple from you afterwards.
You cannot name a man or a boat. Rollo looks at you for a while. 'Then nothing was stolen,' the clerk says for him. 'The count does not hang the river.'
Answer his question first: tell him truly who is on the river behind you

He listens to the count of sails more closely than to the price of anything. That month a strange fleet is turned back at the cliffs. His clerk chalks your casks light, and the missing one is somehow found on the strand.
Let the cask go and say nothing
A cask is not worth a man's neck, even a thief's. Your crew disagree, quietly, as far as the first bend of the river.

A long timber hall by the corner of a Roman wall: a very big old grey-bearded Northman in a Frankish cloak on a bench, an arm ring and an awkward new cross, a young clerk at his elbow, a Frisian standing before them; ships drawn up beyond the open door.
Four pennies a head

The count's court sits in his yard on the island. The abbey of Saint Denis complains that the count's man again asked four pennies a head from strangers at the fair, which King Pippin forbade forty years ago. You were at the landing, and the law-finders want a stranger's word.
Four pennies for a free man, five for a slave. He asked it of the Englishman ahead of you, and of you. I counted. Say what you heard.
My office took that penny before there was an abbot at Saint Denis who could count to four. Speak, shipman. I am listening very closely.
The Frisian who minds his casks. A sound habit.
Say what was asked of you at the landing

The law-finders find for the saint, as their grandfathers did. The count's man is gone from the landing for a few years, and the abbot has your house written down for the freedom of the fair: three Octobers without the saint's toll. The count knows your face now, and not kindly.
Say you were busy with your casks and heard nothing

The count's man nods to you across the yard. The abbey loses nothing but an afternoon, since it has the judgment in its chest. Dominicus says 'four heads' a little louder than he needs to, each time you pass his table.
Ask to hear King Pippin's judgment read before you answer

It is read in Latin and then in the speech of the place: the merchants were staying away, so the king ended the penny. Then the court rises for dinner. You have learned what the law is, and have not yet said on which side of it you stand.

A walled yard beside an old Roman palace: seven law-finders on a bench, a thick-necked count with a grey moustache and folded arms, a small sunburnt toll man with a long notched stick, a Frisian standing alone in the middle; autumn light.
The king's measure

The king's ruling is cried at the saint's landing: the most that may be asked for a measure of oats, barley, rye and wheat, and one new measure for the whole realm. The abbey's toll man has the new measure and is setting every merchant's beside it.
Oats one penny, barley two, rye three, wheat four. And this is the measure: the king's, the same from here to the Saxons. Put yours beside it. Do not be shy, I have seen worse today.
The old measure held less. So the new measure at the old price is a gift, and the old measure at the new price is theft. I explain this forty times a day.
Have your measure checked and marked

Yours is short by two fingers. He has a strip of oak let into the rim and burns the abbey's mark on it with a hot iron. Nobody in the district can now say you sell short, and you can say it of others.
Buy a new measure from the abbey's cooper
Four pennies for a tub of new oak with the mark already burnt in. Dominicus fills it with barley, strikes it level with his stick and pours it back, to show you what a measure is.
Say a Frisian measure has served three generations
He says three generations of buyers would like a word with you. The queue laughs. Your measure stays as it was, and so does his opinion of it.

A river landing below an abbey: a wiry toll man setting two wooden measures side by side on a plank, a branding iron heating in a brazier, a line of merchants with tubs under their arms; bright morning.
Bread at the gate

The abbey of Saint Denis is feeding hundreds at its gate and its barn is nearly empty. The cellarer will buy any grain at the abbey's price, which is low. In the island market the same sack fetches three times as much, and the count's men are watching who asks it.
We baked for three hundred yesterday and it was not enough. Wheat, rye, barley: I take it all, I pay what the abbot allows, and I write your name on a strip which I shall then lose. God will not.
I found the strip with your name. It was in my sleeve the whole time. The abbot has seen it.
Sell two sacks of wheat to the gate at the abbey's price

Eight pennies for two sacks. He taps each one as if it were a cask, chalks it, and has it at the ovens before you are paid. The abbot has your name written where the monks pray for those who did them good.
Sell the wheat in the island market for what it will fetch
Thirty-six pennies, and the buyer thanks you. A man of the count's stands by the stall and counts on his fingers. It is the best week's silver of your year, and it has been seen.
Lend your crew to the ovens for a day

Your four carry wood and water from dawn. A man in the row tells them of the corn that stood in the field and came to dust in the hand. They eat what the row eats, and Waldric loses the note he wrote about it.
The gate of a great abbey: a quick round-shouldered monk with chalk on both sleeves counting sacks, bread ovens smoking behind him, a row of hundreds winding back along the wall; grey summer morning.
Skins by the bundle

At the fair of Saint Denis parchment is sold by the bundle of a hundred leaves. The abbey's cellarer goes from booth to booth, holds each leaf to the light and takes the best. What he passes over is good enough for a school.
Sixty pennies the bundle if there is not a hole in it. I do not bargain. I have not the time, and the saint has the money.
Hold it to the sun. A leaf with a hole was a calf with a fly in its hide. A leaf that is yellow was scraped by a man thinking of his dinner.
The school at Saint-Wandrille takes what I leave, and its master writes me that it had fewer holes than I said. A schoolmaster. Counting my holes.
Buy two bundles of what he passed over
Two hundred leaves, a little yellow, three with holes you can live with. Fifty the bundle. The seller ties them between boards and tells you to keep them drier than yourself.
Sell him the parchment you carry

He holds every leaf to the light, counts a hundred, and pays seventy-two without a word. Then he writes your name on a strip, as one who brings dry skins, and puts the strip in his belt, from which it will fall by evening. He will remember anyway.
Walk the booths with him and learn to judge a leaf

By the sixth booth you can tell calf from sheep by the grain and a careless scraper by the shine. He tells you what a finished book of such leaves is worth, and to whom, and that it is more than your boat.
Tell him, where the abbot can hear, that Ursio of Rotomagus is still unpaid

You say the sum, the number of casks, and the exact words he used last October. The abbot turns his head. Waldric finds the cooper's money in his sleeve at once, with a strip of parchment that says he owed it.

A fairground of booths under an abbey wall: a monk with chalky sleeves holding a leaf of parchment up against a low October sun, bundles tied between boards on a trestle, Frisian and English merchants in the crowd, new wine in open casks.
Martinmas rent
It is Martinmas. The tenants of Saint Germain's bring their wine rent to the abbey in the meadows, and the widow who lodges the Frisians has casks to cart and a carter who began the feast yesterday.
Martinmas, the rent is due in wine, and my carter began the feast yesterday. You have four strong backs doing nothing. I have fed them for a month. I only mention it.
Three casks of rent and one over. Hers is the best that comes in, and I should be obliged if you repeated that to nobody at Saint Denis.
Last Martinmas you rolled my casks to the abbey. This year the bench by the fire is yours and the Englishman can stand.
Roll her casks to the abbey with your crew

Four casks across the Little Bridge and over the meadows, with half the left bank doing the same. The cellarer taps each one and writes it into the abbey's count. Ermentrud walks behind, telling your men how they are doing it wrong.
Keep the feast at her table
Eel, new bread and the wine she kept back from the rent. The sea is shut from today. Your crew eat as if it were the last meal before Lent, which, the way she feeds them, it nearly is.
Ask the cellarer, quietly, for a cask of the rent wine
He looks over both shoulders, though Saint Denis is two hours' walk away, and sells you one cask at thirty-six. He never names the price. He holds up fingers.

Meadows before a great church with a gilded copper roof: men rolling wine casks along a track in a long line, a broad scolding woman with keys at her waist walking beside four Frisians and a cask, a tall stooped monk in a sheepskin tapping casks at the gate; a bright cold November day.
The twentieth October
The widow by the Little Bridge has lodged a Dorestad skipper twenty Octobers and been paid for nineteen. She holds one of his cloaks against the twentieth, and wants word carried to him.
Thiadbod of Dorestad. You know him? Everyone knows him. Twenty Octobers under this roof and nineteen paid for, and I have his second-best cloak in the chest until he remembers.
It is a Frisian cloak. Too short to be worth selling, the Franks tell me. So you see it is not greed. It is the principle.
Did you tell him? What did he say? No, do not soften it.
Promise to tell him at Dorestad
She gives you the message in her own words and makes you repeat it. It is short. The last word of it is 'boy'.
Pay his twentieth October yourself

Ten pennies. She wraps the cloak for you to carry home to him and remarks that a man who owes a widow is a fool, and a man who owes a rival skipper is a fool with company. Thiadbod now owes you, and will be told so along the whole river.
Sit down to the eel and hear what the Frisians said at her table

She tells you what you ate last time, and then what three shipmasters said over the same dish. The fair is short of Frisian cloth this year: two boats that should have come did not. Whoever has bolts to show will not need to shout.

A house by a small timber bridge on an island: a broad woman lifting a short grey cloak out of a chest and shaking it at arm's length, a table with a dish of eels, the river and a moored boat through the open door; evening.
A man who knows the loops
On the strand under the island wall a river man with his own pole and no boat is looking for a berth. He says he knows every loop of the Seine down to the tide.
The river makes five great loops between here and the tide, and a stranger loses a day in each. I lose none. My master sold his barge at the fair's end and did not sell me with it.
I have never seen the sea. I am told it is the same, only wider.
Take him on
He steps aboard with his pole and his bundle and at once tells your steersman where the sand lies. Your steersman has opinions about this. By the second loop he has fewer.
Pay him to take you down to the tide and no further

Six pennies. He takes you down by the inside of each bend and names every mill and landing as it passes. At the tide's head he steps off onto another man's barge and is gone upriver before you have moored.
Ask him the loops and what each costs

He cannot help telling you, for nothing: the long loop by the saint's abbey, the shoal below the second island, the place where the current sets you on the bank. You remember about half of it, which is half more than you knew.

A sandy strand under the wall of an island city: a lean barefoot man leaning on a long pole worn pale at the grip, a bundle at his feet, looking a small sea boat over with interest; barges beyond, low sun.
The abbot's psalter

Abbot Fardulf of Saint Denis receives merchants who carry for the abbey. He asks every boat bound down the river the same thing: a psalter of the abbey's has been at Rotomagus for nine years, with the cathedral's chief singer.
You go down by Rotomagus? Then ask the canon Hildhard for our psalter. Ask kindly. I have asked kindly for nine years, so you may also try the other way.
I came north with a beaten king and I owe everything to this one. I say so before I am asked. It saves time.
You have it? In the boat? Among the casks? Bring it here in your own hands, and do not run.
Promise to ask at Rotomagus
He tells you what it looks like: red boards, a brass clasp, and on the first leaf a great B with a bird in it. He knows it as a man knows a child who was sent away to be fostered.
Put the psalter into his hands

He opens it at the great B with the bird and stands a long time. Then forty pennies, the abbey's thanks, and a place for your name in its book. He looks for damage and finds only that nine years of choir boys have learned their psalms from it.
Tell him the psalter was in your boat and is gone

He does not raise his voice. He has the loss reckoned in pennies by the cellarer, who for once does not lose the note, and has it read to you. No church on the Seine will give your boat a book while he lives.
Hear the verses he has made for the king
They are about a house he built for the king beside the abbey, and they are better than you expected and longer than you hoped. He watches your face throughout. You keep it still.

A bright abbey church with many windows: a lean dark-eyed abbot in a good black habit holding a red-boarded book open at a great painted initial, a Frisian standing before him with wet boots; candles and gold beyond.
Boatmen in the stone
Men digging a footing by the bishop's church have struck carved stones deep under it: a row of men with shields, as in a boat, and a god with a stag's horns. A clerk is telling them to fill the hole.
Look: men in a row, shields along the side, and letters over them. Somebody paid a mason well for that, when there were masons.
It is nothing. Old stones from the time of idols. Fill it in before the bishop walks by, and say an Our Father while you shovel.
Give the diggers a penny to leave it open till dusk

Your crew climb down and look for a long time at men who worked this river before any saint came to it. The priest, in spite of himself, spells out the letters: the boatmen of this people set this up, at their own cost, when a Tiberius was emperor. Then he has it buried.
Help them fill it in
Four more shovels make short work of it. The priest thanks you and says the ground here is full of such things, and that it is best not to dig deeper than a grave.
Say a prayer for all boatmen, theirs and yours
Nobody can say what god those men rowed for. Your steersman says it does not matter: a river is a river, and somebody should ask for them. The priest hears and decides he has not heard.

A deep trench beside a small old cathedral: a block of pale stone carved with a row of bearded men holding shields and a horned god above, half cleared of earth; diggers leaning on shovels, a priest pointing at the hole, Frisian sailors crouched at the edge.
The dyers' roots
A grower from up the river has madder roots dried and bagged, and the dyers he sells to have gone to the fair without him. He will sell cheap to a boat.
Red. The best red this side of the Rhine, dug in the third year. The dyers pay twelve a sack for it. I will take eight, today, because the cart is borrowed.
Honey also. Two crocks. My wife says not under twenty.
Buy three sacks of madder
Three sacks of dry red root that stains your hands through the cloth. The Frisian dyers at home will want it, and so will the English, who make the cloaks the king complains of.
Buy a crock of honey
Twenty pennies, and he will not go under, because his wife will ask. It is dark honey from the lime trees, sealed with a bladder and a twist of straw.
Tell him where the dyers' booths stand at the fair
He thanks you, whips up the borrowed ox and sets off north. With luck he will get his twelve. He owes you a word, he says, the next time you want to know what grows where.

A market between an old palace and a church: a farmer in a patched tunic sitting on the tail of an ox cart with open sacks of dark red roots, two honey crocks between his feet; a Frisian rubbing a root between stained fingers.
Under the tower

The Northmen's great fleet lies below the bridges and the city is shut. A young monk on the wall wants to know who you are and where you stood. The count's men want two things: grain brought in from above, and word carried out.
You, in the boat! Your name, your town, and where you stood on the day the tower burned. I am writing it all down. Somebody must.
Twelve men held the tower by the Little Bridge when the flood broke the bridge behind them. Twelve. I have their names. Do you want to hear them? You shall hear them.
The Frisian who brought wheat down the upper water. You are in book one. Not by name: the metre would not have it.
Sell the count your wheat

The count's steward pays forty pennies for two sacks and would pay it again. Men carry them up through a postern with shields over their heads. Abbo asks which saint you prayed to on the way down, and writes the answer.
Carry the count's word out by the upper river

A strip of parchment sewn into your belt, for whoever holds the next bridge upstream: how many are left, how much bread, how long. You go out at night under the far bank with muffled oars. Behind you somebody on the wall is singing a psalm, badly.
Hear the twelve names

He says them like a psalm: Ermenfred, Eriveus, Eriland, Odaucer, Ervic, Arnold, and six more. They fought until the tower burned under them and were killed after they had been promised their lives. He does not explain a single hard word this time.

An island city wall in winter, smoke over it: a thin young monk with a wax tablet leaning out between the timbers of a rampart, shouting down to a small boat under the bank; far downstream, beyond a broken bridge and a burnt tower, a river crowded with long ships.
Saint John's eve
It is Saint John's feast. Pilgrims have come in from far cities, the night before is a vigil at his church by the cathedral, and every gate of the city stands open.
A feast is not a market, so I take no toll on what a pilgrim carries for his own use. You would be surprised what a pilgrim needs for his own use. Six bolts of cloth, one of them told me.
We walked from Angers. Eleven days, with my mother. She wants to keep the vigil and I want to sit down. Is that your boat? Could a person sit in it?
The bishop frets about open gates on a feast, with a west wind up the river. I tell him the count has men. The count tells him the same. He goes on fretting.
Keep the vigil at the saint's church with your crew

A night of psalms and candle smoke among people who have walked eleven days to be there. Any man of yours who keeps the old gods stands at the back with his arms folded, and stays to the end. In the morning the whole city smells of bread.
Sell to the pilgrims from the boat

Pilgrims buy small and pay well: a knife, a length of cloth, a comb for a mother. Fourteen pennies over what the market would give. The toll man watches from his bench and takes the tenth of it, feast or no feast.
Let pilgrims sleep aboard for a penny each
Six of them, packed like herring among the casks, and one old woman who snores like a saw. They bless the boat in the morning. Your steersman says he has had worse cargoes and quieter ones.

Midsummer dusk inside a Roman city wall, the cathedral roof behind: a small church with every door open and candles inside, a river of pilgrims with staffs, a square Frankish toll man on his bench watching bundles go by, a west wind blowing up the street.
Skins for Tours

On the island of Indre below the city an English monk of Saint Martin's at Tours buys calfskins for the abbey's scribes and looks for boats to carry finished books north. He is exact about books and hopeless about boats.
You are from the north? Truly north? Have you been to York? No. Well. Nobody has. What do you carry, and is any of it calfskin?
A book is the skins of a herd and a year of a scribe, and it is worth more than your boat. I do not say so to wound you. I say so that you will not stow it under the salt.
My abbot collects what the old poets wrote. He has heard there is a book of verses at Bordeaux, in a widow's keeping. He would pay for a true copy, and better than for wine.
You carried Sigewine? Was he sick? He was sick. We were boys in the same school at York. Did the bag reach the bishop?
Your hides made eleven gatherings of a gospel book. I thought you might like to know where your cattle went.
Take his order for calfskin: eight bundles of hides

Eight bundles before the scribes sit idle. He writes it on his tablet, counts the days aloud, loses count, begins again. He pays more than the tanners do, because a tanner has never waited on a bishop.
Sell him the hides you carry

He turns every hide over, looking for the bite of a warble fly, and takes the bundle at twenty. The ferryman poles them over to the island with the monk sitting in the bow, very still, as he has been told.
Hand him the copy of the Bordeaux poet

He reads the first leaf standing in the mud of the landing. A hundred and forty pennies, on the abbot's account, and a letter for the widow in his most careful Latin. The scribes at Tours will copy it again in their clear new hand, and it will be read aloud to men who know the metre.
Ask him what a book is worth, and to whom

He tells you by the skin, by the scribe's month and by the cover. Then to whom: a new bishop in the north will give silver, a heathen will give silver for the cover alone, and the monks it was stolen from will give gold. He stops, and says he should not have told you the last.

A low green island in a wide brown river, a small monastery of timber and stone: a lean fair monk with ink to the knuckles and a wrapped book under his arm, counting bundles of pale calfskin on a landing stage; a ferryman waiting with a pole.
A name in the cart

Count Wido has ridden through all Brittany and come home with a cart of the chiefs' weapons, each cut with its owner's name, to lay before the king. The list was read aloud in the count's yard. The ferryman at the Reze crossing asks whether a certain name was in it.
You had business in the count's yard. You heard the names read. I only ask what any man there could hear.
My mother's brother's lord. A chief by the salt pans at Batz. Was his spear in the cart?
If it was, he has bowed, and his people sell salt to Franks in peace. If it was not, somebody gave up another man's spear. Either way I should like to know before he does.
Tell him the list as you heard it

You say the names in the order they were read. He hears the one he was waiting for, looks at the water, and poles you over without asking his fare. On the bay, by the next moon, the salt masters know there is a Frisian who repeats what he hears and nothing more.
Tell the count that the ferryman is asking
Wido is courteous. He pays thirty pennies, has a word said at the toll bench, and asks you to go on listening where you buy salt. Paternus ferries you after that for the full fare and not one word.
Say you were watching your casks, not listening
He laughs before you have finished the sentence, not after. He takes his fare. He will ask again, sideways, the next time the tide gives him the chance.

A broad river crossing at low water, sandbanks showing: a short thick-armed ferryman in a hooded cape of oiled wool leaning on a pale ash pole, not looking at the Frisian he is speaking to; far off on the city bank, a cart under guard.
The beam of chalk strokes
The ale-house by the carters' gate keeps every salt man's reckoning in chalk strokes on a beam. Its keeper knows who owes whom in the port, and who is about to sell cheap because of it.
A new face and a dry one. Sit. I chalk a stroke a cup on that beam, under your own mark. What is your mark? A boat. They are all boats.
The toll man comes every evening and has done for ten years. I charge him full measure. He seems to like it.
Two salt masters from the bay owe me since Easter and their tubs are full. They will sell under the gate price this week, to anyone with coin, before I send the carter for it.
You paid the English monk's carters off my beam. He went red to the ears. I have not enjoyed anything so much since Lent.
Ask which salt masters are selling cheap

She names them, and where their tubs stand. They sell to you at three sacks for the price of four and are glad to, since the other buyer on offer is her carter. It is true word, and it will not last past Saint Luke's.
Pay off the English monk's carters from her beam

Five pennies, and she wipes a whole row of strokes off the beam with her sleeve. The monk hears of it within the day, comes to thank you, cannot find the words in any of three tongues, and blesses the boat instead.
Drink on the beam and settle when you sail
She chalks your strokes under a little boat with a crooked mast. By the third cup your own crew are telling her things you did not know they thought.

A low ale-house by a city gate: a strong quick woman with a chalk on a string round her neck marking strokes on a roof beam, carters and salt men on the benches, a square Frankish toll man alone with a full cup; a salt shed through the back door.
The stopped doorway
Bishop Gunhard takes you to see an old doorway in the city wall, stopped long ago with loose rubble. He asks what you saw on the Rhine: how long there is between the first sail and the fire.
You are of Dorestad. Then you have seen it. I do not ask to be comforted. How long, from the first sail on the river to the first roof alight?
The clerk at Rotomagus writes the same as you say, and in the same order. Two witnesses. In my calling that is enough to act on.
This doorway was stopped before my time. A man could pull it down with his hands. What do masons cost where you come from?
Tell him plainly: less than a morning
He listens with his whole face and writes nothing down. Then he walks the length of the wall with you, counting the places where one man could not stop three. There are more than he has men.
Give a hundred pennies toward masons for the doorway

A hundred pennies is two masons and their lime for a month. By midsummer the doorway is walled a man's height in mortared stone. It is not the whole wall. It is the place where the rush would have come.
Say the Loire is wider than the Rhine and the count has men
He thanks you for the kindness. He says the bishop of Rotomagus was told much the same thing, by a kind man, in the spring of his own fire.

The inside of a Roman city wall: a slight grey-tonsured bishop in a faded green chasuble with his hand on a doorway filled with loose rubble, weeds growing in it, a Frisian beside him looking up at the height of the wall; a west wind, gulls.
Natan's sons
Nine people of Bordeaux and a chest of scrolls came ashore here from your boat. The city they left has burned. The sons of the man who paid you with a promise have come down to the port to keep it.
Our father said: the Frisian took a debt in place of silver, with the Danes' fires in sight. He said to pay it before we bought a single cask. Here it is, weighed twice.
We trade from this river now. Salt, wine, and what comes from Spain when anything does. What you leave with us we sell in the dear season, and we do not forget whose boat it was.
Take the silver

Three hundred pennies, in good coin of the old weight, counted on a cloth. The younger son writes it off a tablet as it is paid. They ask you to eat with them, and you learn what a household carries when it carries only what matters.
Take half, and leave half with them to trade for your house

A hundred and fifty now, and a hundred and fifty put into salt in your house's name, on a split tally. The elder son says their father will like this better than the paying. A debt paid ends a thing, he says, and a stake begins one.

A hired house by a river port: two young men in long dark belted gowns counting silver onto a cloth, a wax tablet beside it, an old woman and children in the doorway behind, a locked chest against the wall.
The book on the altar

The cathedral of Nantes has been washed of blood and Mass is said in it again. The great Bible that went downriver on a captive's neck lies on the altar, salt-stained along one edge. The canons have sent for the master of the boat that brought it.
We have no bishop. We have this book, and the man who carried it, who will not let anyone else turn its leaves. And we have a debt to a Frisian.
Your house's name is written in the margin, small, by the Gospel for Saint John's day. Nobody will read it out. Everybody who reads that Gospel will see it.
Take what the canons can pay
A hundred and fifty pennies now, in coin, plate being a thing the cathedral no longer has. The rest when the rents come in, if the rents come in. They mean it. You can see what it costs them.
Tell them to put it toward buying their people back
The canon does not argue. He writes a second thing in the margin, under the name. In every street of the city somebody will know whose child came home on silver that a Frisian did not take.

A stripped cathedral with a broken door hanging: a great book open on a bare altar, one edge stained white with salt, a gaunt clerk standing guard beside it, a handful of people who were bought back standing at the front; one lamp.
Oil for three lamps

The island has salt and little else this hungry year. The corn sacks in the cellarer's store hang slack, the oil ship from Bordeaux has not come, and three lamps have burned at the founder's head since he died.
Nine jars empty, two full. The corn you can count yourself: it will not take long. What have you aboard? No: first what you have, then your name.
For a sack of rye I give four of salt. For a jar of oil, twelve. No market on the mainland gives that. No market on the mainland has three lamps to keep.
The third lamp burns on your oil. I filled it myself. I have cut your mark on the doorpost of the store, low down, where the abbot does not look.
You sold on the sand, to the rakers. They ate. I do not say it was wrong. I say I count your sacks twice now.
Sell him two sacks of rye for salt
Eight sacks of grey salt for two of rye, measured level, and he hangs the corn from the beams himself, out of reach of the mice. The house eats bread this week because of it. He says so, once.
Sell him a jar of oil for salt

He carries the jar into the church in his own arms. The keeper holds the wick and Vitalis pours, and neither says a word until the third lamp is burning. Then twelve sacks of salt, and the best of the heap.
Sell the rye to the rakers on the sand, who offer more
Eleven sacks for two, heaped and not level, because the rakers are hungrier than the monks. The widow who leads them calls you her son. The cellarer hears of it before the tide has turned.
Promise him oil from Bordeaux

He names the seller at Bordeaux, a soft-spoken man who is owed for nine jars and has not stopped the next. Two jars, he says, before the autumn gales. He will pay half as much again as oil is worth, in salt or silver, and does not say which he has.

A dim stone storehouse: a thin monk with oil stains to the elbow pointing along a row of tall clay jars, most of them tipped empty, slack corn sacks hanging from the beams; through the door a church with a faint glow inside and salt heaps on the sand.
The salt brother

The brother who keeps the salt will not hand over a sack without setting a riddle first. He has a leaf sent from Quentovic, the second of four, and gives it only to someone who has answered the first.
Salt? Certainly. But first: once I was water, full of scaly fish. Fire tormented me. Now I am most like snow. What am I? You are standing in me to the ankles.
You have my cask leaf. I pour the cups of Bacchus, and I am never drunk. Well? What am I?
A cask! Split with wedges by a countryman, and full of what makes men foolish. You have cost me an evening's sport. The next leaf is with a Frisian wine shipper at Mainz.
The old abbot in the guest house corrects my Latin and will not give me his answers. He says a monk who cannot name a cask has no business in a cellar.
Answer the salt riddle

He laughs, wipes his hands on his habit and brings out the leaf: a thing split with wedges by a countryman, that pours the cups of Bacchus and is never drunk itself. It is Latin. He throws in a sack over the measure, for the pleasure of being answered.
Answer the cask riddle

He claps the salt off his hands and gives you eight pennies from the store, with the cellarer's tally cut for it. Then the name of the man at Mainz who has the third leaf, and a request: if you ever come back, read him the next one.
Guess, wrongly, and buy salt at the common price
He shakes his head with real regret and sells you salt like anyone else. Each time you call he will ask again, a little more gently, as one asks after a sick relation.

Clay salt beds shining under a low sun: a sunburnt barefoot monk, his black habit white to the knee, leaning on a long wooden rake and holding a folded leaf just out of a Frisian's reach; grey heaps of salt, a monastery behind.
The emperor's cousin

The old emperor's cousin, Abbot Adalard of Corbie, lives in the island's guest house as the new emperor's exile, with a king's man by the door. On the second evening, while the watcher eats, he asks whether your boat calls at Quentovic.
Tell me about the toll at Dorestad. Who takes it, at what rate, and what he does when a man swears his cargo is an abbey's. I ask exact questions. Bear with me: it is all I am allowed.
My own house is on the Somme. A letter from here goes by the Canche: there is a monk of ours on the abbeys' row. Can you keep a thing dry? And yourself?
The count at Nantes pays for knowing who carries the old abbot's letters, and to whom. I do not threaten. It is only a question of which lord a merchant wants to be known to.
Take the letter for Quentovic
It is folded small and tied with a knot his own monks will know. He does not tell you what it says. He tells you the name of the man on the abbeys' row, and that the man will ask you about wax.
Take it, and tell the watcher

The watcher reads it by the kitchen fire. It asks after a brother, a sister and the state of the granaries. He pays you forty pennies all the same, on the count's account, and ties the knot again, very nearly right.
Tell him plainly you will not carry it

He nods. A merchant must know his own hold, he says, and goes on asking about tolls. He will find another ship before the summer is out. His talk of the court stays open to you, and it is worth hearing.

A plain guest-house room with a small window on the sea: a tall spare old monk with white hair round his tonsure, a small book in his left hand, speaking low to a Frisian; in the doorway beyond, a man in a riding cloak bent over a bowl.
A book the length of a hand
The exile has seen your sail from the guest-house window. He is at the west gate before you are, and the watcher is a little way behind him.
You are back. Wait. Do not tell me yet whether it is dry. Let me hold it first.
The clerk on the Canche has read it, I think. The stitching is not ours. Well. He will have learned a great deal about bees.
Give him the book

He weighs it in his hand, opens it, and reads the first page standing in the wind. Then he has ten sacks of the house's best salt put aboard and tells you what such a book is worth: nothing in a market, and to the right house more than a field. When he is abbot again, his cellarer will buy from you first.
Give him the book, and ask what is in it

He reads to you from it, putting the Latin into plain speech: how many loaves for the gate, who keeps the mill, where the bees stand, what the porter says to a stranger. It is the ordering of a house. He says a boat is a house, a small one, and that you seem to keep yours.
Tell him it is gone
