He looks at the sea for some time. He says he wrote it once and can write it again, being given the leisure. He does not ask you into the guest house, and the salt brother keeps his riddles to himself for a year.

A monastery gate on a windy island: a tall old monk standing on the path with a small linen-sewn book open in both hands, reading, his habit blown against his legs; a Frisian with his sea chest open at his feet, a watcher further up the path.
On the sand
On the sand by the salt heaps the islanders trade for what the monks do not buy: needles, knives, cloth, a pot. The widow who leads the rakers has a neighbour's son beside her who wants to go to sea.
My son, you have iron in that boat, I can smell it. Knives? Needles? The monks buy oil and corn. We are the ones who need a knife.
This heap is this week's. That one is last year's, swept up. I tell you because you would find out, and then you would not come back.
I know the ebbs. I can pole, bail and keep quiet. My mother says the sea took my father and may as well feed me.
The knives you sold us cut. That is not as common as you would think.
Trade a crate of iron tools for salt

Fourteen sacks, heaped, from this week's heap. She tries each knife on her thumbnail before she takes it. The rakers carry the salt down to the boat themselves, so that you can see nobody swaps a sack on the way.
Take the lad on
He comes aboard with nothing but a knife on a string. Maura tells you his mother's name and says that if he drowns you are to come and say so yourself. She says it laughing. She means it.
Let her show you which heap is which
New salt is grey and damp and smells of the sea. Last year's is whiter, harder, and has sand in it that you find with your teeth. It is knowledge worth a penny a sack at any market north of here.

A wide grey beach with heaps of salt under rush thatch: a strong loud woman in a kilted brown dress with a rake over her shoulder, trying a knife on her thumbnail; a thin barefoot boy beside her, Frisians unloading a crate; low tide, big sky.
The clerk in the salt hut

The fleet that stormed Nantes on Saint John's day lies in the shell bay, sharing its plunder on the sand and fighting over it. In the salt hut, under the rakes, the islander is hiding a clerk of the cathedral with its great Bible strapped to his body.
Lie on the lagoon side, not in the bay. They have been killing each other over the spoil since yesterday. They want bread and wine and pay in things that came off altars.
They hung it on my neck to carry to the ships. When the sea drew back and the guards were fighting, I walked. I have not put it down. I do not think I can.
I cannot keep him past the next daylight ebb. Tonight there is a little water on the lagoon side, and no moon.
Take the clerk and the book off on the night ebb

You pole out over a hand's depth of water with the clerk lying on the bottom boards and the book on top of him. Nobody sees. By first light the island is a line behind you, and he is still holding the straps.

She touches once on the lagoon bar, and a shout goes up from the bay. Two arrows, a thrown spear, a man of yours cut along the arm. Then the ebb has you and they have other quarrels. The clerk has not let go of the straps.
Buy altar plate in the bay, by weight

Two pieces for eighty pennies' weight, from a man with blood on his sleeve who does not haggle. It is the cheapest silver you will ever buy, and it cannot be shown in a Christian market without a story. The clerk is found at the next ebb. Martinus sells you salt afterwards and does not ask you into the hut.
Load salt on the lagoon side and ask nothing

You are one of the few who still sail for salt, and with the Loire shut it will fetch double on the Seine and the Canche this year. You never learn what became of the clerk. The chronicle says he got away.

Inside a dark rush hut among salt rakes: a gaunt clerk crouched with a book as big as a door strapped across his chest, a lean sun-dark islander at the door watching the shore; beyond, far off, long ships in a bay and smoke; evening.
Windbound at Conca
Ships lie in the shell bay waiting for a wind, fed by the monks for charity. The island's pilot sits on an upturned boat watching the water, and says the channel to the monastery dries twice a day.
Wait. There. See the colour change? That is the bar. In an hour a child could walk it. In six you could sail a church over it.
A flat sea in summer is a road for anyone. I liked it better when I was only afraid of weather.
The pilot at the Garonne mouth is a friend of mine. We have never met. If you go south, tell him Ursus says his river is still a ditch, and give him this bread.
You paid me in silver last time. The monks pay in bread. I can eat both, but only one of them keeps.
Hire him over the bar on the next flood

He stands in the bow with his ringed pole and says nothing for an hour, then one word, then nothing. You never feel the bar. He steps off at the bay's mouth into a boy's skiff with a loaf under his arm for the man at the Garonne, and no opinion of your steering that he will give away free.
Wait for the wind with the others and share the monks' bread

A Breton salt boat, a Bordeaux wine boat and you, three days in a bay shaped like a shell. The porter brings bread at noon and asks nothing. The masters trade prices from three rivers, which is worth more than the bread.
Ask him to name the marks, and say them back

The wood on the east head over the church roof; the three great stones on the north-west point; the place where the water goes pale. He makes you say them back twice, and corrects the order. He names days by the moon and distances by tides, and by the end so do you.

A shell-shaped bay with three small ships at anchor: a broad short pilot with a face like a boot sitting on an upturned boat, a sounding pole ringed with red wool across his knees, pointing with his chin at a change of colour in the water; a monastery on the low island behind.
The pilot's fee

The old pilot who brought you through the banks of the river mouth is waiting at the gate. He has piloted the count's boats for three seasons on a promise, and would like his fee from you in silver, before you sell.
The channel was there yesterday. I do not say it is there today. I say you are here, so it was. Six pennies, at the gate, before the wine sellers have your purse.
At the big tides of the low river a wave comes up ahead of the flood, as high as a man's knee, sometimes his belt. Lie in midstream with your head to it, or it will put you among the vines.
You paid at the gate. I have told my grandson: that boat, the small one, you take first.
You promised, like the count. He at least has a hall to hide in.
Ursus sends bread and an insult? Then he is alive. Tell him the Garonne has more water in its mud than his bay has in its sea.
Pay him at the gate
He counts the six pennies on his fingers as he counts tides, and puts them in his cheek. Then he tells you, unasked, which wine seller waters and which only says the others do.
Pay him, and two pennies over for his grandson to teach you the marks

The boy walks you along the bank at low water and names each bar as it shows: where it was last year, where it is now, where his grandfather thinks it is going. It is not the whole river. It is the part that kills strangers.
Promise to pay when the cargo is sold
He nods slowly. He never says a thing is safe, only that it was yesterday, and he seems to think the same of promises. He will take you down again. He will take the others first.

A muddy river bank under a four-square wall of grey stone: a lean stooped old man, brown as a nut, in a sleeveless goat-hair cloak, leaning on a sounding pole taller than himself ringed with red cord, his hand out; a wide brown river, boats aground at low water.
The poet of the city

The widow who keeps the house by the Broken Tower has one old book: the verses a man of this city made when Rome still ruled, about Bordeaux and every other famous city. On a slow evening she reads from it to the room.
Sit. You are in the house of people who were senators when your people were frogs. I say it without malice. Wine?
He says of this city: walls four-square, towers so high they pierce the clouds, and the tide of the ocean coming up the river with a sea of fleets. It is still true. Less the fleets, until you.
An English monk at the Loire has written to ask for a copy, in careful Latin, for the abbot at Tours. One clerk at Saint Andrew's writes a fair hand. He wants skins, ink and forty days.
Is it read at Tours? Aloud? By men who understand the metre? Then you shall have the good cask. No, I will pour.
Listen to the end

She reads a line and puts it into plain speech, and so on through twenty cities none of your crew will ever see. Nobody on the benches speaks. When she shuts the book she looks round as if daring anyone to have enjoyed it less than she did.
Pay for the copy and carry it to the Loire

The clerk has been at it since the letter came: the copy wants only its last gathering and your forty pennies for the skins. She asks twice who it is for before the leaves go out of her house. She wraps it herself, in a cloth that was her mother's.
Tell her the news of the Loire and the Franks
She corrects two of your place names and one king. Then she tells you who slept in the city last night and why, which is better news than yours.

An old stone house built into a broken Roman tower: a small upright white-haired woman in a dark veil reading aloud from an open book on her knees, a ring with a red stone on her finger, benches of shipmen and vine-dressers listening, wine jars along the wall; lamplight.
Oil for the island
Oil comes up from the south by river and cart and is dear this year. The seller knows the island of the three lamps: its monks owe him for last year's jars, and no oil ship has gone north.
Forty the jar. Do not make that face: it was fifty at Easter. Taste. Where are you bound?
The salt island? Then listen. Forty measures went there in their founder's day. They owe me for nine jars. I have not stopped the next ones. I have only not found a boat.
They tell me the third lamp is burning again, on oil that came in a Frisian boat. I should like to think it was mine.
Buy two jars outright
Seventy-six for the two, since you did not haggle long. He wedges them upright in your hold with his own straw and tells you that if one cracks he would like the pieces.
Stand surety for the monks, and carry four jars on their account

Sixty pennies down against the old debt, and four jars go aboard on the island's tally with your mark beside the cellarer's. The monks will pay you in salt, at a rate no mainland market gives. He says he would not be the man who put a lamp out, and now he need not be.
Ask what he would give for bay salt
More than you thought. The salt boats from the bay are late this year and the fish at the river mouth will not wait. He tells two neighbours you asked, and by evening the price on the bank has moved.

A market by a silted Roman harbour inside a city wall: a plump soft-spoken man with oiled grey hair dipping a rod into a tall clay jar, a string of little tasting spoons at his belt, rows of jars wedged in straw; warm southern light.
The count's leave

Count Seguin holds the city for King Louis and the river against the Gascons on the far bank. Nobody trades across the water without his leave, and he gives it for a gift, for news of the king, or not at all.
What does it cost? No, do not tell me what it is. What does it cost? Then I shall know whether I want to know what it is.
Across the river are Gascons. They have horses and hides and no manners. Sell them cloth and salt. Sell them one mail coat and I hang you from your own mast, and it is a short mast.
They tell me Wido has taken the Bretons' spears and laid them before the king in a cart. A cart! I have held this river since before he could ride, and I get letters about my manners.
The Frisian with news. You told me where the king was, and it was true. Sit, then.
Give him a gift for his leave

He weighs the silver in his hand and does not count it, which is his way of saying it will do. The far bank is open to your house, and the man at the water gate is told to look the other way more often than not.
Tell him where the king is, and what the Franks say in the north
He wants the king's whereabouts, then the price of horses, then whether anyone in the north has said his name. You answer the first two. He takes the third answer from your face.
Ask what a horse fetches south of the Loire
More than a man, he says, and less than a mail coat, and he is buying both. By morning every dealer on the bank knows the count asked a Frisian about horses, and prices themselves accordingly.

A walled enclosure with a timber hall inside an old city: a thick-necked count in a red tunic with a hawking glove in his belt, sitting sideways on a bench, a sword on a baldric; behind him an open gate onto a wide river and a far, low, wooded bank.
Nine people and a chest

The Danes have lain round the wall for months. At the water gate a wine and salt dealer of the city asks passage to the Loire for nine people and a chest of scrolls. He will pay in wine, in silver, or in a debt his sons will honour. Others at the gate watch whom you take.
Nine people. My mother, who will complain. Four children, who will not. And a chest that must not get wet. I have read enough to know who is blamed when a wall fails.
I can pay in wine at a third of its price, tonight, from my own cellar. Or in a debt. My sons will be alive to honour it, if you say yes.
Take the nine and the chest out on the night ebb

Nine people sitting on one another, a chest on the bottom boards, no cargo. You drop down on the ebb past the fires with the oars muffled, and the old woman does not complain until Blaye is astern. Then she makes up for it.

A fire boat's crew see you against the glow. Arrows in the dark, one of your men hit, a child crying and hushed. Then the ebb takes you round the bend. The chest is dry. The old woman binds the wound herself and says nothing at all.
Buy his wine at a third and run it out alone
Three casks for the price of one, carried down to the water gate by his own sons. He thanks you for the silver, which will be of use to him, and goes on down the bank to the next boat.
Tell him your boat is too small for nine
It is true. He says so himself. He looks at the boat a moment longer, as a man reckons a thing he would have tried anyway, and goes to ask a Breton.

A water gate in a city wall at night, the sky upriver lit by camp fires: a tall narrow man in a long dark gown with his hand on a child's shoulder, an old woman, a small heavy chest carried by two youths, a very small boat at the foot of the steps.
